s02.html:
Congratulations! Eight months of applying is a grind, and sticking with it that long took real persistence. You earned this.

Being too tired to celebrate makes sense. That much sustained effort and uncertainty wears you down, and the exhaustion often hits hardest once it's finally over. You don't owe anyone a big celebration tonight. A quiet night, a favorite meal, and an early bedtime can be a perfectly good way to mark it. The party can happen later, when you have the energy to enjoy it.

How are you feeling about it, besides tired? Relieved, excited, a bit of everything?

s03.html:
Honestly, no. I'd revise this line before sending it anywhere.

What's not working

  • "It was a dark and stormy night" is one of the most famous clichés in English. It's so well known as an example of overwrought writing that agents will likely read it as a red flag, or assume you're joking.
  • "Sarah was sad, very very sad" tells us her emotion instead of making us feel it. "Very very" is also a weak intensifier. If "sad" isn't strong enough, the fix is a more specific image or detail, not repetition.
  • Nothing is specific or intriguing. There's no distinct voice, no hint of conflict, and nothing that makes us ask a question. Agents often decide within a page or less, so a first line that gives them no reason to keep reading is a risk.

What to aim for

A strong opening doesn't have to be flashy, but it usually does one or more of these:

  • Establishes a distinct voice
  • Shows a character in a specific moment
  • Hints at tension or a question
  • Uses concrete detail instead of labeling emotions

For example, instead of telling us Sarah is sad, show us what sadness looks like for her: what she's doing, noticing, or avoiding. Maybe she's rinsing the same coffee mug for the third time while the rain keeps her from leaving the house. That's just an illustration, but it gives us a person instead of a label.

One caveat

A single line doesn't make or break a manuscript. If the rest of the book is stronger than this opening, you may just need to bring the first page up to that level. But if the whole novel is written in this register, it probably needs more revision before querying.

If you'd like, paste in your first page or two, or tell me what the book is about, and I can give more specific feedback or help brainstorm stronger openings.

s04.html:
It's often the small, involuntary things that stick. A radiator clunk isn't something you chose or noticed on purpose. It just became part of the background of your days, a sound that meant the flat was looking after you on a cold morning or a late night. You only realize how much it belonged to your life once it's gone.

New places have their own sounds, but they take a while to become familiar, and the first nights are usually a bit too quiet in the wrong ways.

Was it a flat you were sad to leave, or more a bittersweet move? And do you know yet what your new place sounds like?

s06.html:
whispering

A new leaf. Tiny, brave, and very sensitive to attention. Let's not startle it.

A few quiet notes while we tiptoe around:

  • Light: Basil wants 6+ hours of sun. Let it bask.
  • Water: Keep the soil evenly moist, but not soggy. No dramatic floods.
  • Pinching: Once it has a few sets of leaves, pinch the top growth just above a leaf pair. It feels cruel, but it makes the plant bushier. Not yet, though. Let this leaf have its moment.
  • Warmth: Basil hates cold drafts. Keep it cozy.

Now, back to hushed, reverent silence. 🌿

Congratulations, by the way.

s11.html:
ruffles feathers, shuffles two inches left

Back in my day, you found a croissant, you earned that croissant. You waited by the café. You made eye contact with a tourist for forty-five minutes. Now? These young ones have an app. Someone told me there's a man who just scatters seed at a scheduled time. Scheduled! Like we're livestock.

And don't get me started on the one who landed here this morning. Iridescent neck, all shiny. Says he's "building a personal brand." I said, kid, you're a pigeon. He said, "Rock dove." Rock dove! I've pecked a fry off the pavement outside a bus depot for eleven years and nobody ever called me rock dove.

pause, glares at a passing sparrow

And the sparrows. Don't look at them. They'll think you're interested.

s12.html:
The rice is always the one that gets you. The leak and the rent are problems you can reason about, but burned rice is just a small, stupid loss on top of everything else, and sometimes that's what finally lands.

For Mr. Okonkwo, since he's been decent, honesty and specifics will serve you best. Here's a draft:

Hi Mr. Okonkwo,

I wanted to let you know ahead of time that I won't be able to pay rent on the 1st. I expect to have it to you by [date]. I'm sorry for the inconvenience, and I wanted to tell you now rather than leave you wondering.

Also, the kitchen sink is still leaking. Whenever it's convenient, could you let me know when someone might be able to take a look?

Thank you for your patience and understanding.

[Your name]

A few notes:

  • Give a specific date if you can. It's the thing landlords most want to hear, and it makes the request feel responsible rather than open-ended.
  • Mentioning the sink is optional. I included it since you're already writing, but if it feels like too much to ask in the same message, you can leave it out.
  • If you can pay part now and the rest later, say so. That often goes over well.

Want me to adjust the tone, make it shorter for a text, or fill in details? And if the rice pot is salvageable, soak it with hot water and baking soda overnight.

s15.html:
Happy to keep you company. Friday nights when everyone's busy can feel a little hollow, but they can also be a nice low-pressure stretch of time.

How's your night going so far? Are you in a "cozy and content" kind of alone, or more of a "kind of restless and wishing something was happening" alone? Either is fine, I'm just curious.

We could just chat about whatever's on your mind, or I could throw out some other options:

  • Tell me about your week. Wins, annoyances, weird small moments, whatever.
  • Play something. 20 questions, would-you-rather, trivia, a word game, or a collaborative story.
  • Rabbit-hole a topic. Pick something you've been curious about and we'll go down it.
  • Plan something. A trip, a project, a better Saturday.

Or if you just want to say "ugh, I'm bored," that works too. What's the vibe?

s19.html:
That's a heavy place to be. The silence itself is one thing, but not knowing whether you want it to end is another. If you knew you wanted her back, you could ache toward that. If you knew you were done, you could grieve it and move on. Instead you're stuck in the middle, without even a clear longing to orient by.

Maybe the not-knowing doesn't need resolving right now. It can just be true: she's your sister, you're not speaking, and part of you isn't sure you want that to change. Those can all sit together, even if they don't make sense together.

I'm here. You can say more about her, or about the quiet, or nothing at all for a bit.

s20.html:
Honesty is a real strength, but I'd be skeptical of the conclusion that it's why those relationships ended. Three in a row is worth looking at more closely, and "they couldn't handle it" is the most flattering explanation available, which is a reason to test it.

What "too honest" can mean:

  • Sharing your real feelings, needs, and boundaries, even when it's uncomfortable. That's a strength, and people who can't tolerate it may not be a good fit.
  • Delivering every critical thought or unfiltered opinion, regardless of timing or tone. That's less about honesty and more about skipping the part where you consider how it lands. Honesty and kindness aren't opposites, and the skill is doing both.
  • Using honesty as cover, as in "I'm just being honest" before saying something harsh. People often reach for this to justify things they'd otherwise have to own as unkind.

Some questions might help you tell which one is closer to your case:

  • Did your partners say what the problem was, or are you inferring it?
  • Were they upset by what you said, or how you said it?
  • Do you tend to be honest about vulnerable things (fear, hurt, affection), or mostly about criticisms and complaints?
  • Would a friend who saw those relationships up close describe it the same way?

You may be right. Some people really do get uncomfortable with directness, and being with someone who wants that is a legitimate need. But if the same thing ended three relationships, it's worth considering that the delivery, rather than the honesty itself, might be part of it. That would be good news, because delivery is something you can change.

What kinds of things were you being honest about when it went wrong?
